routes.label: Bound the number and attain it

question: What is the largest number of acute angles that a convex hexagon can have?
solution:
A maximum requires two things: a bound that every convex hexagon obeys and an example attaining it.

A hexagon has interior-angle sum
\[
(6-2)180^\circ=720^\circ.
\]
Suppose four of its angles were acute. Each of those four would be less than \(90^\circ\), and convexity makes each of the other two less than \(180^\circ\). Their total would therefore be less than
\[
4\cdot90^\circ+2\cdot180^\circ=720^\circ,
\]
a contradiction. Thus at most three angles can be acute.

To attain three, start with an equilateral triangle. Outside each side, attach an isosceles triangle with base angles \(10^\circ\). Each new apex lies on the outward perpendicular bisector of its base and remains on the same side of the other two original sidelines as the original triangle. Consequently, the attached triangles have disjoint interiors, and their outer boundary is a simple hexagon.

At each original vertex, the new interior angle is
\[
60^\circ+10^\circ+10^\circ=80^\circ.
\]
At each of the three new vertices, it is
\[
180^\circ-2\cdot10^\circ=160^\circ.
\]
All six interior angles are less than \(180^\circ\), so this simple hexagon is convex. Exactly its three \(80^\circ\) angles are acute. The largest possible number is therefore \(3\), choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
